On the economic front, consumer sentiment fell more than expected in October's initial reading as inflation expectations accelerated.

On Wednesday, CPI data for September will be released with Retail sales and PPI data for the month the following day; initial jobless claims are also due on Thursday. data.title: IG: Guide To The Principal Investment Grade Corporate ETF
data.description:
The Principal Investment Grade Corporate ETF (IG) is an actively managed fund of investment-grade corporate bonds, as its name suggests. Principal aims to beat a broad corporate index by buying bonds priced low compared with similar ones.

This overview covers IG’s structure and holdings, its potential place in a portfolio, performance history, how it might respond in different markets, and peers.

How Is IG Structured?

IG is actively managed. It doesn’t track an index, though Principal’s stated goal is to beat the Bloomberg US Corporate Investment Grade Index. That index holds about 8,800 bonds.

At least 80% of net assets must be in investment-grade corporate bonds and other fixed income. Investment grade means a rating of BBB- or higher from S&P, or Baa3 or higher from Moody’s. (When the two conflict, the higher one counts.) Unrated bonds are left to the managers’ judgment. The fund can also hold U.S. government debt, foreign corporate bonds, and foreign government bonds payable in dollars.

Duration is an estimate of how much a bond’s price moves when rates change: a duration of seven years means a 1-point rise in rates cuts the price by about 7%. IG’s duration has to stay within 10% of its benchmark’s in either direction. The Bloomberg’s was 6.7 years on June 30, 2026, which put IG’s allowed range at roughly 6.0 to 7.4 years.

The managers can adjust duration with Treasury futures instead of buying or selling bonds. Those are exchange-traded contracts that rise and fall with Treasury prices. The managers can also use credit default swaps, which pay out if a borrower defaults, and credit index futures. Both can add/reduce exposure to a sector or company. In the year ended June 2026 the managers’ trades equaled 80.5% of the portfolio’s value.

IG launched in April 2018 as the Principal Investment Grade Corporate Active ETF and dropped “Active” from the name in April 2026. It has ~$202 million in assets. The expense ratio is 0.19% with monthly distributions.

What’s in the Principal Investment Grade Corporate ETF Portfolio?

IG had 263 holdings on September 30. Seeking Alpha’s top ten, as of August 31, totals 22.6% of assets:

Six of the ten lines are corporate bonds, and together they’re 8.9%. The other four aren’t bonds. Two are Treasury futures (listed at the full value of the Treasuries they track) and another is a State Street government money market fund IG uses for cash. The fourth, “other assets less liabilities,” covers unsettled trades and accrued interest.

Morningstar’s list from October looks different:

It has a futures line but no cash lines. Futures positions change as the managers adjust duration. The 2-year Treasury future was 4.55% of assets on Seeking Alpha’s August list and 7.17% on Morningstar’s October list. Principal’s own top ten leaves out futures and the money market fund.

Four of the six bonds on Seeking Alpha’s list are from banks, and banks, brokers, and insurers made up ~41% of the portfolio on June 30. Principal’s list shows those four bank notes as “VAR” (short for variable). Each pays a fixed coupon until a set date, then switches to a floating rate.

On August 31 about 60% of the bonds were rated BBB, the lowest investment-grade letter grade, and 2.5% were BB. Those figures come from Principal’s credit chart. For that, Principal adds Fitch to S&P and Moody’s and uses the middle ratings. (Under the prospectus only S&P and Moody’s count, and the higher rating applies.) A bond rated BBB- by S&P, Ba1 by Moody’s, and BB+ by Fitch shows as BB on the chart but still counts as investment grade under the prospectus.

As of September 30, average effective maturity was 12.6 years and duration was 6.31 years. IG trades actively, so the bonds and their weights will look different each time these pages update.

How Might IG Fit in a Portfolio?

Corporate bonds pay more than Treasuries because the borrower can default or be downgraded. IG’s recent yield to maturity was 6.27%. A 7-year Treasury, with a duration of about 5.8 years, yielded 5.19%. The 1.08-point gap is the spread.

How much IG changes a portfolio depends on what’s already owned. The iShares Core US Aggregate Bond ETF (AGG) had 24.7% in corporate bonds on October 7 and a duration of 5.68 years vs. IG’s 6.31. Adding IG to AGG or Vanguard’s (BND) mostly raises the corporate share. There’d be little change in overall rate sensitivity. Someone holding only T-bills would be adding credit risk and rate risk at once. Someone holding only 30-year Treasuries would be adding credit risk and lowering rate risk.

An IRA or 401(k) suits IG better than a taxable account. Corporate bond interest is taxed as ordinary income, and unlike Treasury interest, it’s subject to state income tax.

How Has IG Performed Since Inception?

IG has returned an average of 2.15% a year since launch:

Over the same stretch, the corporate index IG tries to beat returned ~2.33% a year. The gap of ~0.18 points is close to the 0.19% fee, so before the fee IG was about even with its index. The Bloomberg US Aggregate (which adds Treasuries and mortgage bonds to corporates) returned ~1.5%. IG beat its index in four of seven calendar years.

Interest rates explain the chart’s big moves except those in 2020. In March of that year Treasury yields reached record lows but IG fell as investors dumped corporate bonds and spreads widened. Then the Fed announced it would buy corporate bonds, and Q2 2020 became IG’s best quarter at +10.29%. The 2022 drop came as the Fed raised rates. IG lost ~16.9% that year vs. ~15.8% for its index.

Payouts account for more than all of the return. The share price fell ~22% from $25 at launch to $19.50 in early October 2026. Reinvested payouts covered that drop and produced the whole gain on top of it. Over the past 12 months, IG paid $1.042 a share, ~5.3% of the $19.50 share price. Monthly amounts over the last three years ranged from $0.078 to $0.101.

In a taxable account, federal taxes on the payouts took nearly the entire return. Through 2024, the latest period Principal reports, IG’s 2.04% annual return since launch fell to 0.02% after taxes on distributions at the top federal rate.

How Might IG Perform in Different Markets?

Rising rates lower IG’s price by the duration math described earlier, and the interest it earns offsets part of the loss. In Q3 2026, oil prices tied to the U.S.-Iran war raised inflation fears, and the Fed raised rates in September. IG’s yield to maturity rose 0.87 points, to 6.27%. The duration math puts the price loss at about 5.5%. Interest earned during the quarter, ~1.35%, offset part of it, and IG finished down ~4.04%. Falling rates work in reverse. The share price rises, but monthly distributions shrink as maturing bonds are replaced with lower-yielding ones.

IG has held more BBB-rated bonds than its index. Their spreads are wider and move more than higher credit quality. From October 9, 2023, to September 30, 2026, the spread on ICE’s BBB corporate index narrowed from 1.58 points to 1.03. The single-A index narrowed from 1.11 to 0.72. When spreads widen, the gap works against IG.

Banks made up ~30% of IG on June 30 vs. ~22% of the index. A selloff in bank bonds would be a bigger negative for IG than for its index. When Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023, spreads on financial companies’ bonds widened more than in any other sector.

How Does The Principal Investment Grade Corporate ETF Compare to Peers?

Of the active funds below, IG is the only one that covers every maturity and keeps its duration within a fixed range of its benchmark’s (the 10% limit described earlier).

Active, All Maturities, Broad Corporate Index

These are the four closest: actively managed, investment-grade corporate bonds of any maturity, and benchmarked against the index IG aims to beat (or a close relative). The AB Corporate Bond ETF (EYEG) and the Global X Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF (GXIG) pick bonds using quantitative models, and the Franklin Investment Grade Corporate ETF (FLCO) can have up to 40% in foreign issuers. The Fidelity Corporate Bond ETF (FCOR) is measured against the Bloomberg US Credit Index, which adds government-related bonds.

Active, Up to 35% in High Yield

About 16% of the American Century Diversified Corporate Bond ETF (KORP) was recently rated BB or B, the top two tiers of high yield. Its three-to-seven-year duration range isn’t tied to any index.

Active, Split Into Three Maturity Ranges

The PGIM Corporate Bond 0-5 Year ETF (PCS) (0-5 years), the PGIM Corporate Bond 5-10 Year ETF (PCI) (5-10), and the PGIM Corporate Bond 10+ Year ETF (PCL) (10+) each cover one slice of the maturities IG holds together.

Index funds that screen on credit risk and value

The VanEck Moody's Analytics IG Corporate Bond ETF (MIG) favors bonds that Moody’s Analytics scores as both cheap and less likely to be cut to high yield. The iShares Investment Grade Systematic Bond ETF (IGEB) tracks an index that drops the bonds most likely to default; about 76% of the fund was rated BBB on September 25.

Index Funds Tracking IG’s Benchmark

Vanguard’s (VTC) and JPMorgan’s (BBCB) track the index IG aims to beat and charge a fraction of IG’s fee.

Others are less closely related: the iShares iBoxx $ Inv Grade Corporate Bond ETF (LQD) tracks only the most liquid investment-grade bonds. Invesco’s BulletShares and Vanguard’s BondBuilder series hold bonds maturing in a single year; their 2027 funds are the Invesco BulletShares 2027 Corporate Bond ETF (BSCR) and the Vanguard Target Maturity 2027 Corporate Bond ETF (VBCA). The Vanguard Multi-Sector Income Bond ETF (VGMS) allocates 40% to 60% to high yield.

Summary

IG is an actively managed fund of investment-grade corporate bonds whose duration must stay within 10% of the index it aims to beat. The managers can adjust duration with Treasury futures instead of trading bonds. Monthly payouts of bond interest, taxed as ordinary income, have supplied more than all of IG’s return because the share price has fallen. Since launch IG has returned 2.15% a year so far, about even with that index before the 0.19% fee.

This article answered the following questions:

  1. How is IG structured and what does it hold?
  2. How has IG performed, and how might it behave in different markets?
  3. How does IG compare to similar ETFs?

Author’s Note: This analysis reflects data and information available as of October 8, 2026.

Editor's note: This article is intended to provide a general overview of the ETF for educational purposes only and, unlike other articles on Seeking Alpha, does not offer an investment opinion about the ETF.
